ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: In a cross-sectional survey conducted on Prolific, 299 Asian American and 284 Black American adult participants reported their definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality using open-ended responses.

Since correlations of r = .10 stabilize at around 250 data points with 80% confidence (Schönbrodt & Perugini, 2013), 300 U.S. Asian Americans and 300 U.S. Black Americans were sampled on Prolific.com for a total sample size of 600 before exclusions to have adequate power for pairwise and correlational analyses.
table.formatted: Since correlations of r = .10 stabilize at around 250 data points with 80% confidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Schönbrodt & Perugini, 2013)</ref>, 300 U.S. Asian Americans and 300 U.S. Black Americans were sampled on Prolific.com for a total sample size of 600 before exclusions to have adequate power for pairwise and correlational analyses.

table.text: We restricted our sample to adults residing in the U.S., including U.S. non-citizens, with at least a 95% approval rating on Prolific.com.
These participants were removed from all analyses, as pre-registered on OSF.
Multiracial participants were included in the sample, but were a minority in both the Asian American (n = 5; 1.6%) and Black American samples (n = 9; 3.2%).
That said, because all coders were Asian-identified, our subjective lens and data interpretation could be different from those of a team of multiracial or Black American coders.

The overrepresentation of East Asian participants and how participants were categorized may have influenced the themes that emerged, even though it was not our goal to detect within-sample differences.
Finally, several participants provided elaborate, similar nationality definitions, raising the possibility that they consulted external sources.

table.title: Asian and Black Americans' Definitions, Self-labeling, and Self-Identification of Ethnicity, Race, and Nationality
table.research_questions:
Self-labeling: We hypothesize that Asian American participants will report self-labeling to a high extent with ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic (racial), and pan-ethnic (racial) American identity labels (H1a). Asian American participants' self-labeling will be similar across ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic (racial), and pan-ethnic (racial) American identity labels (H1b). Asian American participants will self-label with these label types to a greater extent than with the American label (H1c). Self-labeling across label types will be positively correlated (H1d). 

Self-identification: We also hypothesize that Asian American participants will report higher ethnic identification (EIS) than American identification (AIM) (H2). 

Consistency with Self-identification and Self-labeling: For each racial group, EIS will positively correlate with the us of ethnic and ethnic American identity labels (H3a). AIM will positively correlate with the use of ethnic American, pan-ethnic American, and American identity types (H3b). Race Centrality will positively correlate with the use of pan-ethnic American and pan-ethnic identity labels (H3c). 

Identity Shift Strategies: Black and Asian Americans' use of identity shift strategy will differ from the midpoint (H4).
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview: This study has a correlational design. We will recruit 300 Asian and 300 Black US participants on the behavioral research platform Prolific for enough power to make pair-wise comparisons and test for correlations.
table.randomization: All randomization will be done through Qualtrics using randomization blocks in the survey flow,  randomizing questions at the block level, or randomizing statement order in individual items.  Specifically, we will randomize the order in which participants give their definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality. In a randomized order, participants will report their EIS, AIM, and Race Centrality. We will also randomize at the statement level for these three scales, such that the order of items is random. We will randomize at the statement level for race, ethnicity (Asian and Black), and gender, but "Something not listed" will always be last.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: We will recruit 300 US residents of Asian descent and 300 US residents of Black descent from the online behavioral research platform, Prolific, for a total sample size of 600 before exclusions. We will restrict the sample to participants who are at least 18 years old and have above a 95% rating. We anticipate collecting enough participants within a 2-day timeframe. Participants will be paid $2.67 for a 20 minute survey ($8.00 per hour).
table.sample_size: We will recruit 300 US residents of Asian descent and 300 US residents of Black descent from the online behavioral research platform, Prolific, for a total sample size of 600 before exclusions.
table.sample_size_rationale: This study is a replication (and revision) of Study 2 of the Asian Racial Self-Identification (ARSI) project. The original study was underpowered for most analyses, with a sample size of 31 monoracial White and 23 monoracial Asian students from Harvard’s SONA. Of the Asian sample, 19 participants were monoracial East Asian. For this study, we plan on recruiting 300 Black and 300 Asian participants on Prolific. Given that correlations of .1 stabilize around 250 data points with 80% confidence (Schönbrodt & Perugini, 2013), we aim for at least 250 per group after exclusions. Moreover, for Black and Asian comparisons, we ran a simple power analysis on G*Power using the smallest effect size in the original dataset. An a priori two-tailed t-test can detect an effect size of d = 0.27 (a small-to-medium effect) with .8 power at a significance level of α = 0.05 with a sample size N = 171 per group.
table.stopping_rule: We will run the study on Prolific until we reach 600 participants. To collect two samples (Black and Asian), we must set up two Prolific projects. Each project will stop collecting data when the sample pool reaches 300 accepted responses.
table.measured_variables:
Main Predictor Variables:

Ethnic Identification Scale. We will measure participants' ethnic identification using the full 17-item Ethnic Identification Scale (EIS; Umaña-Taylor et al., 2004). Participants will report the extent to which they have explored their ethnic identity (Exploration; 7 items, e.g., "I have attended events that have helped me learn more about my ethnicity."), the degree to which they have resolved what their ethnic identity means to them (Resolution; 4 items, e.g., "I am clear about what my ethnicity means to me."), and the affect or emotion they associate with their ethnic identity (Affirmation; 6 items, e.g., "I am not happy with my ethnicity," reverse coded) on a 1(Strongly Disagree) to 7(Strongly Agree) Likert scale.

United States Identity Scale. We will measure participants' American identification using the full 17-item United States Identity Scale (USIS; Meca et al., 2019). Participants will report the extent to which they have explored their American identity (Exploration; 7 items, e.g., "I have attended events that have helped me learn more about the U.S."), the degree to which they have resolved what their American identity means to them (Resolution; 4 items, e.g., "I am clear about what being American means to me."), and the affect or emotion they associate with their American identity (Affirmation; 6 items, e.g., "I am not happy with being American," reverse coded) on a 1(Strongly Disagree) to 7(Strongly Agree) Likert scale.

Race Centrality. We will measure the centrality or importance of participants' race using the adapted Race Centrality sub scale of the Multidimensional Inventory of Black Identity (MIBI; Sellers et al., 1997). Participants will report the extent to which race is an important part of their understanding of self (e.g., "In general, being a member of my racial group is an important part of my self-image.") on a 1(Strongly Disagree) to 7(Strongly Agree) Likert scale.

Private Regard. We will measure participants feelings about their racial group using the adapted Private Regard sub scale of the Multidimensional Inventory of Black Identity (MIBI; Sellers et al., 1997). Participants will report the extent to which they view their racial group positively (e.g., "I am happy that I am a member of my racial group") on a 1(Strongly Disagree) to 7(Strongly Agree) Likert scale.

Exploratory (Predictor) Variables:

Self-perceived Prototypicality. We will measure the extent to which participants view themselves as representative of People of Color (PoC), their racial group, their ethnic group, and Americans using the eight-item Self-Perceived Prototypicality Scale (Chin et al., 2022; e.g., "I am similar to the average Person of Color") on a 1(Strongly Disagree) to 7(Strongly Agree) Likert scale.

Intersecting Social Identities. We will measure the extent to which participants view their social identities as overlapping or intersecting using the 28-item Intersecting Social Identities Scale (Westberg & Syed, under review; e.g., "I keep my race/ethnicity, gender, and social class separate") on a 1(Strongly Disagree) to 5(Strongly Agree) Likert scale.

Criterion/Outcome Variables:

Ingroup and Outgroup Identity Shift. Participants will answer the 16-item Ingroup and Outgroup Identity Shift Scale (adapted from Loyd et al., 2023). Participants will report the extent to which they change how they self-present their racial/ethnic/national identity to their ingroup AND outgroup members (e.g., “[I have] changed my behavior to fit in”) and how they feel in reaction to those changes (e.g., "[When experiencing the changes described above, I] experienced positive emotions or feelings.") on a 1(strongly disagree) to 7(strongly agree) Likert scale, and why they altered their self-presentation in a multiple choice response question.

Self-Labeling. Participants will answer a 5-item question about how they self-label in terms of their ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic/racial, pan-ethnic/racial American, and American identities. Participants will report whether they self-label as each identity on a 1(strongly disagree) to 7(strongly agree) Likert scale.

Qualitative Self-Labeling (Open-Ended):

1.	Some people see their racial, ethnic, American identities as interchangeable and/or connected, whereas others see these identities as distinct and/or independent from each other. How would you write your all-encompassing identity that touches upon these domains?

2.	Are there situations where you self-label your racial, ethnic, and American identities one way versus another (For example: as Chinese vs. Chinese American; as Asian vs. Chinese)?

3.	If you change the way you self-label, what, specifically, does this look like?

Quantitative Definitions (Open-Ended):

1. How do you define race?

table.statistical_tests:
Hypothesis 1a: To test whether Asian American participants report self-labeling with ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic, and pan-ethnic American labels to a high extent, we will run a one-sample, one-tailed t-test to test whether the means are greater than the midpoint of the scale, 4. 

Hypothesis 1b: To test whether Asian American participants report similar self-labeling with ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic, and pan-ethnic American labels, we will run a repeated measures ANOVA. We will perform similar analyses for the qualitative open-ended response, counting the number of "hits" of each identity label types and performing repeated measures ANOVA.

Hypothesis 1c: To test whether Asian American participants report greater self-labeling with ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic, and pan-ethnic American labels than American, we will run one-tailed pairwise t-tests. We will perform similar analyses for the qualitative open-ended response, counting the number of "hits" of each identity label types and performing one-tailed pairwise t-tests of each ethnoracial identity label against the American label.

Hypothesis 1d: We will calculate zero-order correlations (Pearson correlation coefficient, r) to test for correlations between identity labels.

Hypothesis 2: We will perform a one-tailed pairwise t-test to test for whether Asian American participants report higher EIS than AIM. 

Hypothesis 3a-c: We will calculate zero-order correlations (Pearson correlation coefficient, r) between EIS, AIM, Race Centrality, and the 5 identity labels. 

Hypothesis 4: We will perform one-sample, two-tailed t-tests for a difference in Black and Asian Americans' identity shift strategies from the midpoint, 4.
table.transformations:
We have three open-ended, qualitative questions. In each question, we will transform qualitative responses into quantitative responses, as counts or "hits."

Question 1: "Some people see their racial, ethnic, American identities as interchangeable and/or connected, whereas others see these identities as distinct and/or independent from each other. How would you write your all-encompassing identity that touches upon these domains?" To test for participants' (qualitative) self-labeling, we will count the number of "hits" for each label using XXX: ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic (racial), pan-ethnic (racial) American, and American.

Question 2: "Are there situations where you label/communicate/express your identity pertaining to race, ethnicity and national identity one way versus another?" We will conduct a hit count analyses for yes/no responses. We will also perform a thematic analyses. Step 1: We will perform inductive coding to identify broad categories of situations where participants alter self-labeling. Step 2: We will count the number of hits for each category generated in Step 1. 

Question 3: "Specifically, how do you change the way you label/communicate/express your identity pertaining to race, ethnicity and national identity?" We will code the qualitative responses in four steps. Step 1: We will do a hit count for shifts FROM ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic, pan-ethnic American, and American labels. Step 2: We will do a hit count for shifts TO ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic, pan-ethnic American, and American labels. Step 3: We will identify notable patterns of shift from Step 1 and Step 2. Step 4: We will code a hit count for shift patterns based on Steps 1-3.

Participant and parent birth origin (e.g., "Where were [you/your mother/your father] born?")  will be transformed into a standardized immigrant generation measurement following recommendations from Baumgartner et al., 2021. According to this recommendation, if a participant and their parent(s) were both foreign-born (1), the participant is classified as first-generation. If a participant is US born (2) and their parents are foreign-born (1), the participant is classified as second-generation. If both a participant and at least one parent are US born (2), they are third (+) generation.
table.inference_criteria: We will use p < .05 as our criteria for statistical inference. For all pairwise comparisons, we will use the "emmeans" package in R, which controls for multiple comparisons.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: We will exclude all participants who fail our attention check. Our attention check is in the demographics, where participants will be asked to indicate the number of fatal heart attacks they have experience. The correct answer is zero.
table.missing_data_handling: We will delete data pairwise if its missing. Thus there might be different numbers of participants in different analyses.
table.exploratory_analyses:
We will test for generational differences in Asian American participants' self-labeling with different identity labels using regressions for each identity types. Agreement with a given identity type (Y) = Intercept + β1*generational status (as a dummy variable) + error. Based on Tovar and Feliciano (2009), second-generation should predict the use of identity types related to American and racial identities. 

We will test for differences in Black American participants' self-labeling with the ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic, pan-ethnic American, and American identity types using repeated measures ANOVA and pairwise t-tests.

We will test for whether levels of self-labeling using each identity label differs between Asian and Black American participants using two sample t-tests for each identity type.

We will test for how Asian American participants' race centrality compares to EIS and AIM (paired t test: EIS-Race Centrality & AIM-Race Centrality).

We will test whether Asian and Black American participants differ in their EIS, AIM, and Race Centrality. For the Black sample, we will perform repeated measures ANOVA and pairwise t tests. For the Asian-Black comparison, we will perform two sample t tests for each identity types.

We will test for the difference between correlations of EIS and ethnic/ethnic American vs. EIS and pan-ethnic/pan-ethnic American, respectively, using the r.test function in the "psych" package in R. Specifically, we will perform a test of significance for the differences between two dependent correlations sharing one variable (William's Test). We will also perform Fisher's Z transformation and compare z-scores. We will do the same for race centrality and pan-ethnic/pan-ethnic labels vs. race centrality vs. ethnic/ethnic American labels. If race and ethnicity are conflated, there will be no differences. 

We will perform correlations among identity shift strategies for ingroup and outgroup shifts, respectively.

For each racial group, we will test what identity shift strategies are more commonly used for ingroup shift and outgroup shift, respectively, using repeated-measure ANOVA and pairwise t-tests.

We will test for racial differences in participants’ engagement in overall outgroup shift and ingroup shift? For this Asian-Black comparison, we will perform two samples t-tests on the overall outgroup shift scores and the overall ingroup shift scores. IF YES: we will test whether there are racial differences in the use of specific strategies using two-sample t-tests for each strategy type.

For each racial group, we will analyze the main motivation for engaging in outgroup shift and ingroup shift, respectively? For each race, we will calculate and compare the % of “gain reward” versus “avoid risk”.

For each racial group, we will analyze what type of emotional response (positive versus negative) each identity shift strategy elicits.

We will perform a binary logistic regression of whether participants express their identity differently in different situations (yes/no) with generational status as the independent variable.

We will perform exploratory thematic analyses of whether the pattern of identity shift (qualitative) changes depending on the situation. 

We will perform exploratory analyses of prototypically as PoC.

table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview: This study has a correlational design. We will recruit 300 Asian and 300 Black US participants on the behavioral research platform Prolific for enough power to make pair-wise comparisons and test for correlations.
table.randomization: All randomization will be done through Qualtrics using randomization blocks in the survey flow,  randomizing questions at the block level, or randomizing statement order in individual items. table.data_collection_procedures: We will recruit 300 US residents of Asian descent and 300 US residents of Black descent from the online behavioral research platform, Prolific, for a total sample size of 600 before exclusions. table.sample_size: We will recruit 300 US residents of Asian descent and 300 US residents of Black descent from the online behavioral research platform, Prolific, for a total sample size of 600 before exclusions.
table.sample_size_rationale: This study is a replication (and revision) of Study 2 of the Asian Racial Self-Identification (ARSI) project. The original study was underpowered for most analyses, with a sample size of 31 monoracial White and 23 monoracial Asian students from Harvard’s SONA. Of the Asian sample, 19 participants were monoracial East Asian. For this study, we plan on recruiting 300 Black and 300 Asian participants on Prolific. Given that correlations of .1 stabilize around 250 data points with 80% confidence (Schönbrodt & Perugini, 2013), we aim for at least 250 per group after exclusions. Moreover, for Black and Asian comparisons, we ran a simple power analysis on G*Power using the smallest effect size in the original dataset. An a priori two-tailed t-test can detect an effect size of d = 0.27 (a small-to-medium effect) with .8 power at a significance level of α = 0.05 with a sample size N = 171 per group.

table.measured_variables:
Main Predictor Variables:

Ethnic Identification Scale. We will measure participants' ethnic identification using the full 17-item Ethnic Identification Scale (EIS; Umaña-Taylor et al., 2004). Participants will report the extent to which they have explored their ethnic identity (Exploration; 7 items, e.g., "I have attended events that have helped me learn more about my ethnicity."), the degree to which they have resolved what their ethnic identity means to them (Resolution; 4 items, e.g., "I am clear about what my ethnicity means to me."), and the affect or emotion they associate with their ethnic identity (Affirmation; 6 items, e.g., "I am not happy with my ethnicity," reverse coded) on a 1(Strongly Disagree) to 7(Strongly Agree) Likert scale.

United States Identity Scale. We will measure participants' American identification using the full 17-item United States Identity Scale (USIS; Meca et al., 2019). Participants will report the extent to which they have explored their American identity (Exploration; 7 items, e.g., "I have attended events that have helped me learn more about the U.S."), the degree to which they have resolved what their American identity means to them (Resolution; 4 items, e.g., "I am clear about what being American means to me."), and the affect or emotion they associate with their American identity (Affirmation; 6 items, e.g., "I am not happy with being American," reverse coded) on a 1(Strongly Disagree) to 7(Strongly Agree) Likert scale.

Race Centrality. We will measure the centrality or importance of participants' race using the adapted Race Centrality sub scale of the Multidimensional Inventory of Black Identity (MIBI; Sellers et al., 1997). Participants will report the extent to which race is an important part of their understanding of self (e.g., "In general, being a member of my racial group is an important part of my self-image.") on a 1(Strongly Disagree) to 7(Strongly Agree) Likert scale.

Private Regard. We will measure participants feelings about their racial group using the adapted Private Regard sub scale of the Multidimensional Inventory of Black Identity (MIBI; Sellers et al., 1997). Participants will report the extent to which they view their racial group positively (e.g., "I am happy that I am a member of my racial group") on a 1(Strongly Disagree) to 7(Strongly Agree) Likert scale.

Exploratory (Predictor) Variables:

Self-perceived Prototypicality. We will measure the extent to which participants view themselves as representative of People of Color (PoC), their racial group, their ethnic group, and Americans using the eight-item Self-Perceived Prototypicality Scale (Chin et al., 2022; e.g., "I am similar to the average Person of Color") on a 1(Strongly Disagree) to 7(Strongly Agree) Likert scale.

Intersecting Social Identities. We will measure the extent to which participants view their social identities as overlapping or intersecting using the 28-item Intersecting Social Identities Scale (Westberg & Syed, under review; e.g., "I keep my race/ethnicity, gender, and social class separate") on a 1(Strongly Disagree) to 5(Strongly Agree) Likert scale.

Criterion/Outcome Variables:

Ingroup and Outgroup Identity Shift. Participants will answer the 16-item Ingroup and Outgroup Identity Shift Scale (adapted from Loyd et al., 2023). Participants will report the extent to which they change how they self-present their racial/ethnic/national identity to their ingroup AND outgroup members (e.g., “[I have] changed my behavior to fit in”) and how they feel in reaction to those changes (e.g., "[When experiencing the changes described above, I] experienced positive emotions or feelings.") on a 1(strongly disagree) to 7(strongly agree) Likert scale, and why they altered their self-presentation in a multiple choice response question.

Self-Labeling. Participants will answer a 5-item question about how they self-label in terms of their ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic/racial, pan-ethnic/racial American, and American identities. Participants will report whether they self-label as each identity on a 1(strongly disagree) to 7(strongly agree) Likert scale.

3.	If you change the way you self-label, what, specifically, does this look like?

table.statistical_tests:
Hypothesis 1a: To test whether Asian American participants report self-labeling with ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic, and pan-ethnic American labels to a high extent, we will run a one-sample, one-tailed t-test to test whether the means are greater than the midpoint of the scale, 4. 

Hypothesis 1b: To test whether Asian American participants report similar self-labeling with ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic, and pan-ethnic American labels, we will run a repeated measures ANOVA. We will perform similar analyses for the qualitative open-ended response, counting the number of "hits" of each identity label types and performing repeated measures ANOVA.

Hypothesis 1c: To test whether Asian American participants report greater self-labeling with ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic, and pan-ethnic American labels than American, we will run one-tailed pairwise t-tests. We will perform similar analyses for the qualitative open-ended response, counting the number of "hits" of each identity label types and performing one-tailed pairwise t-tests of each ethnoracial identity label against the American label.

Hypothesis 1d: We will calculate zero-order correlations (Pearson correlation coefficient, r) to test for correlations between identity labels.

Hypothesis 2: We will perform a one-tailed pairwise t-test to test for whether Asian American participants report higher EIS than AIM. 

Hypothesis 3a-c: We will calculate zero-order correlations (Pearson correlation coefficient, r) between EIS, AIM, Race Centrality, and the 5 identity labels. 

Hypothesis 4: We will perform one-sample, two-tailed t-tests for a difference in Black and Asian Americans' identity shift strategies from the midpoint, 4.
table.transformations:
We have three open-ended, qualitative questions. In each question, we will transform qualitative responses into quantitative responses, as counts or "hits."

Question 1: "Some people see their racial, ethnic, American identities as interchangeable and/or connected, whereas others see these identities as distinct and/or independent from each other. How would you write your all-encompassing identity that touches upon these domains?" To test for participants' (qualitative) self-labeling, we will count the number of "hits" for each label using XXX: ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic (racial), pan-ethnic (racial) American, and American.

Question 2: "Are there situations where you label/communicate/express your identity pertaining to race, ethnicity and national identity one way versus another?" We will conduct a hit count analyses for yes/no responses. We will also perform a thematic analyses. Step 1: We will perform inductive coding to identify broad categories of situations where participants alter self-labeling. Step 2: We will count the number of hits for each category generated in Step 1. 

Question 3: "Specifically, how do you change the way you label/communicate/express your identity pertaining to race, ethnicity and national identity?" We will code the qualitative responses in four steps. Step 1: We will do a hit count for shifts FROM ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic, pan-ethnic American, and American labels. Step 2: We will do a hit count for shifts TO ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic, pan-ethnic American, and American labels. Step 3: We will identify notable patterns of shift from Step 1 and Step 2. Step 4: We will code a hit count for shift patterns based on Steps 1-3.

Participant and parent birth origin (e.g., "Where were [you/your mother/your father] born?")  will be transformed into a standardized immigrant generation measurement following recommendations from Baumgartner et al., 2021. According to this recommendation, if a participant and their parent(s) were both foreign-born (1), the participant is classified as first-generation. If a participant is US born (2) and their parents are foreign-born (1), the participant is classified as second-generation. If both a participant and at least one parent are US born (2), they are third (+) generation.

table.data_exclusion_criteria: We will exclude all participants who fail our attention check. Our attention check is in the demographics, where participants will be asked to indicate the number of fatal heart attacks they have experience. The correct answer is zero.
table.missing_data_handling: We will delete data pairwise if its missing. Thus there might be different numbers of participants in different analyses.
table.exploratory_analyses:
We will test for generational differences in Asian American participants' self-labeling with different identity labels using regressions for each identity types. Agreement with a given identity type (Y) = Intercept + β1*generational status (as a dummy variable) + error. Based on Tovar and Feliciano (2009), second-generation should predict the use of identity types related to American and racial identities. 

We will test for differences in Black American participants' self-labeling with the ethnic, ethnic American, pan-ethnic, pan-ethnic American, and American identity types using repeated measures ANOVA and pairwise t-tests.

We will test for whether levels of self-labeling using each identity label differs between Asian and Black American participants using two sample t-tests for each identity type.

We will test for how Asian American participants' race centrality compares to EIS and AIM (paired t test: EIS-Race Centrality & AIM-Race Centrality).

We will test whether Asian and Black American participants differ in their EIS, AIM, and Race Centrality. For the Black sample, we will perform repeated measures ANOVA and pairwise t tests. For the Asian-Black comparison, we will perform two sample t tests for each identity types.

We will test for the difference between correlations of EIS and ethnic/ethnic American vs. EIS and pan-ethnic/pan-ethnic American, respectively, using the r.test function in the "psych" package in R. Specifically, we will perform a test of significance for the differences between two dependent correlations sharing one variable (William's Test). We will also perform Fisher's Z transformation and compare z-scores. We will do the same for race centrality and pan-ethnic/pan-ethnic labels vs. race centrality vs. ethnic/ethnic American labels. If race and ethnicity are conflated, there will be no differences. 

We will perform correlations among identity shift strategies for ingroup and outgroup shifts, respectively.

For each racial group, we will test what identity shift strategies are more commonly used for ingroup shift and outgroup shift, respectively, using repeated-measure ANOVA and pairwise t-tests.

We will test for racial differences in participants’ engagement in overall outgroup shift and ingroup shift? For this Asian-Black comparison, we will perform two samples t-tests on the overall outgroup shift scores and the overall ingroup shift scores. IF YES: we will test whether there are racial differences in the use of specific strategies using two-sample t-tests for each strategy type.

For each racial group, we will analyze the main motivation for engaging in outgroup shift and ingroup shift, respectively? For each race, we will calculate and compare the % of “gain reward” versus “avoid risk”.

For each racial group, we will analyze what type of emotional response (positive versus negative) each identity shift strategy elicits.

We will perform a binary logistic regression of whether participants express their identity differently in different situations (yes/no) with generational status as the independent variable.

We will perform exploratory thematic analyses of whether the pattern of identity shift (qualitative) changes depending on the situation. 

We will perform exploratory analyses of prototypically as PoC.

live_data_statements: In a cross-sectional survey conducted on Prolific, 299 Asian American and 284 Black American adult participants reported their definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality using open-ended responses.

Since correlations of r = .10 stabilize at around 250 data points with 80% confidence (Schönbrodt & Perugini, 2013), 300 U.S. Asian Americans and 300 U.S. Black Americans were sampled on Prolific.com for a total sample size of 600 before exclusions to have adequate power for pairwise and correlational analyses.
We restricted our sample to adults residing in the U.S., including U.S. non-citizens, with at least a 95% approval rating on Prolific.com.
These participants were removed from all analyses, as pre-registered on OSF.
Multiracial participants were included in the sample, but were a minority in both the Asian American (n = 5; 1.6%) and Black American samples (n = 9; 3.2%).
That said, because all coders were Asian-identified, our subjective lens and data interpretation could be different from those of a team of multiracial or Black American coders.

The overrepresentation of East Asian participants and how participants were categorized may have influenced the themes that emerged, even though it was not our goal to detect within-sample differences.
Finally, several participants provided elaborate, similar nationality definitions, raising the possibility that they consulted external sources.

text.text: Research on ethnicity, race, and nationality often conceptualizes and measures these identities independently, overlooking their interconnectedness.

Perceptions of, and associations among, these identities could differ across racial groups, given distinct migration and racialization contexts in the U.S. Furthermore, nationality has not been thoroughly explored in ethnicity and race research.
This study examined how individuals from groups with different migration and racialization histories (i.e., Asian and Black Americans) define ethnicity, race, and nationality.

In a cross-sectional survey conducted on Prolific, 299 Asian American and 284 Black American adult participants reported their definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality using open-ended responses.
The definitions were thematically analyzed and reviewed between-and within-group variations.

Definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality shared similarities between samples: ethnicity by cultural components or family and ancestry; race by shared physical, genetic, and biological traits; and nationality by birthplace, belonging, and affiliation.
Geographic locations also defined all three identities.
However, Asian Americans commonly perceived ethnicity as narrower than race.
Black Americans viewed the two identities as interchangeable and more frequently defined race as a social construct.
Nationality had more ties to citizenship for Asian Americans than for Black Americans.
Improved theorization and measurement of ethnic, racial, and national identity and the explicit inclusion of national contexts when discussing ethnic-racial identities are necessary.

Despite being routinely theorized about, measured, and controlled for in psychological research, ethnicity, race, and nationality can be difficult to define as independent identities, due to overlapping conceptualizations in lay terms and as constructs.

We argue that research needs improved conceptualization to address a) the distinct meanings of these identity domains and their permeable boundaries; b) the implied U.S. context in most ethnicity and race research and the subsequent omission of nationality from the broader intellectual discourse; and c) the unique migration and racialization (i.e., the social process of acquiring a racial identity) contexts of social groups in the U.S. Each of these issues contributes to potentially different understandings of ethnicity, race, and nationality among social groups.

Approaching ethnicity, race, and nationality as independent identities that uniformly apply across social groups likely leads to fragmented theory and measurement, misleading group comparisons, overlooked within-group heterogeneity, and limited explanatory power for minoritized social groups' experiences (Helms et al., 2005; Schwartz et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Approaching ethnicity, race, and nationality as independent identities that uniformly apply across social groups likely leads to fragmented theory and measurement, misleading group comparisons, overlooked within-group heterogeneity, and limited explanatory power for minoritized social groups' experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Helms et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Schwartz et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: To move research towards more nuanced conceptualizations of ethnicity, race, and nationality, we examined how individuals from two minoritized groups with distinct migration and racialization contexts in the U.S. (i.e., Asian and Black American adults) understand these identities and their relationships.
Ethnicity often denotes groups sharing ancestry, culture, beliefs, and memories of migration or colonization (e.g., Vietnamese, Somali; Cornell & Hartmann, 2007).
text.formatted: Ethnicity often denotes groups sharing ancestry, culture, beliefs, and memories of migration or colonization (e.g., Vietnamese, Somali; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Cornell & Hartmann, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Race (e.g., Asian, Black) is a culturally structured, systematic way of understanding and experiencing reality, dividing humans into groups based on physical appearance, sociopolitical factors, and cultural backgrounds (Smedley & Smedley, 2007).
text.formatted: Race (e.g., Asian, Black) is a culturally structured, systematic way of understanding and experiencing reality, dividing humans into groups based on physical appearance, sociopolitical factors, and cultural backgrounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Smedley & Smedley, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Driven by oppression and hierarchy, racial formation is an evolving, dynamic process (Omi & Winant, 2014; Yamamoto, 1995).
text.formatted: Driven by oppression and hierarchy, racial formation is an evolving, dynamic process <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Omi & Winant, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Yamamoto, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: For example, until 2024, individuals of Middle Eastern descent were federally classified as "White" due to strategies by early immigrants to circumvent discriminatory U.S. policies restricting immigration to "White persons" (Takaki, 1989).
text.formatted: For example, until 2024, individuals of Middle Eastern descent were federally classified as "White" due to strategies by early immigrants to circumvent discriminatory U.S. policies restricting immigration to "White persons" <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Takaki, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike ethnicity and race, nationality is characterized by formal rules, such as a government that sets boundaries and rules for membership.
However, informal criteria (e.g., customs) can legitimize one's claim to national membership, and individuals can have allegiance with a nation without formal membership (Schildkraut, 2014).
text.formatted: However, informal criteria (e.g., customs) can legitimize one's claim to national membership, and individuals can have allegiance with a nation without formal membership <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Schildkraut, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Nationality is also fluid, as the underlying land (and thus the people who live on it), can belong to different nations over time.
For instance, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) transferred California from Mexico to the U.S., altering its residents' nationality.
While these formal definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality are conceptually distinct, both lay people and researchers often connect these terms.

Their distinctions blur further when ethnicity and nationality become racialized, as seen in the misconception that all Black people are from African nations, or that American-ness equates to White-ness (Devos & Banaji, 2005; Winston & Kittles, 2005).
text.formatted: Their distinctions blur further when ethnicity and nationality become racialized, as seen in the misconception that all Black people are from African nations, or that American-ness equates to White-ness <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Devos & Banaji, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Winston & Kittles, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Also, these boundaries shift considerably with sociopolitical contexts: racial bans on citizenship for Black people were forced open after the Civil War, and later for Asian Americans following civil rights struggles throughout the mid-20th century (Takaki, 1989).
text.formatted: Also, these boundaries shift considerably with sociopolitical contexts: racial bans on citizenship for Black people were forced open after the Civil War, and later for Asian Americans following civil rights struggles throughout the mid-20th century <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Takaki, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: However, existing research struggles to study ethnicity, race, and nationality in tandem, often treating them as separable.

This separationist approach is rooted in Western psychology's empiricist traditions that, in pursuit of scientific credibility, operationalize interconnected psychosocial experiences as discrete, orthogonal constructs (Loevinger, 1957).
text.formatted: This separationist approach is rooted in Western psychology's empiricist traditions that, in pursuit of scientific credibility, operationalize interconnected psychosocial experiences as discrete, orthogonal constructs <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Loevinger, 1957)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, it prevents an intersectional understanding of racialization, such as why ethnic groups in the same racial category can experience discrimination differently (Bhakta, 2022).
text.formatted: Consequently, it prevents an intersectional understanding of racialization, such as why ethnic groups in the same racial category can experience discrimination differently <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bhakta, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: With these issues in mind, some scholars have advocated for joint theorization of ethnicity and race, which are commonly entangled in people's minds.

For example, immigrant and racially minoritized groups are simultaneously assigned racial labels by their host society and also maintain ethnic identification rooted in their heritage (Rivas-Drake & Umaña-Taylor, 2019).
text.formatted: For example, immigrant and racially minoritized groups are simultaneously assigned racial labels by their host society and also maintain ethnic identification rooted in their heritage (Rivas-Drake & Umaña-Taylor, 2019).

text.text: This integration represents a meaningful departure from previous decades of scholarship that treated ethnicity (e.g., Phinney, 1992) and race (e.g., Sellers et al., 1998) as two parallel processes.
text.formatted: This integration represents a meaningful departure from previous decades of scholarship that treated ethnicity (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Phinney, 1992)</ref> and race (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Sellers et al., 1998)</ref> as two parallel processes.

text.text: However, operationalizing ethnicity and race into a single construct often prevents discerning the distinct meanings people ascribe to ethnicity and race and articulating how people construct meaning by comparing and contrasting their ethnicity and race.

A methodological example of this limitation is the Ethnic Identity Scale (EIS; Umaña-Taylor et al., 2004), which collapses ethnicity and race into one ethnic-racial identity, maximizing cross-group applicability but limiting insights into how individuals navigate these two distinct axes of identity.
text.formatted: A methodological example of this limitation is the Ethnic Identity Scale (EIS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Umaña-Taylor et al., 2004)</ref>, which collapses ethnicity and race into one ethnic-racial identity, maximizing cross-group applicability but limiting insights into how individuals navigate these two distinct axes of identity.

text.text: Research on ethnicity and race frequently omits nationality, but national contexts determine the status of ethnic and racial groups.
For example, Asian Americans are cast as the "perpetual foreigner" in the dominant U.S. narrative (Zou & Cheryan, 2017), rendering their claims to U.S. sociopolitical membership conditional.
text.formatted: For example, Asian Americans are cast as the "perpetual foreigner" in the dominant U.S. narrative <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Zou & Cheryan, 2017)</ref>, rendering their claims to U.S. sociopolitical membership conditional.

text.text: By comparison, while Black Americans' formal U.S. membership is less questioned, the root of that membership is forced migration and slavery, making Black American's relationship with their nationality strained (Ogbu, 1978).
text.formatted: By comparison, while Black Americans' formal U.S. membership is less questioned, the root of that membership is forced migration and slavery, making Black American's relationship with their nationality strained <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Ogbu, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, Black American's civic and social participation remains hindered (Zou & Cheryan, 2017).
text.formatted: Furthermore, Black American's civic and social participation remains hindered <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Zou & Cheryan, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, nationality is not a neutral backdrop, as it carries different meanings for different groups, and thus should be meaningfully included in ethnicity and race research.
From a metascience perspective, ethnicity and race research is epistemically bound to the national context in which it is generated.
Rooted in settler-colonialism, the U.S. has justified privileges of select social groups by asserting their superiority over other groups (Takaki, 1989).
text.formatted: Rooted in settler-colonialism, the U.S. has justified privileges of select social groups by asserting their superiority over other groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Takaki, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Early race research in the U.S. served White supremacy, supporting eugenics and claims of innate differences among racial groups to justify systematic mistreatment and oppression of racially minoritized groups (Gould, 1981).
text.formatted: Early race research in the U.S. served White supremacy, supporting eugenics and claims of innate differences among racial groups to justify systematic mistreatment and oppression of racially minoritized groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Gould, 1981)</ref>.

text.text: Even with the increased focus on ethnicity, culture, and socialization stemmed from the Civil Rights Movement and the shift from conceptualizing race as biologically determined to socially constructed, race continues to have an organizing role in sustaining power in the U.S. (Omi & Winant, 2014).
text.formatted: Even with the increased focus on ethnicity, culture, and socialization stemmed from the Civil Rights Movement and the shift from conceptualizing race as biologically determined to socially constructed, race continues to have an organizing role in sustaining power in the U.S. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Omi & Winant, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: To sum, the U.S. context dictates both the importance of ethnicity and race, and the research generated about them.
Ironically, this U.S.-centric focus reinforces the invisibility of nationality in ethnicity and race research, limiting its utility across national contexts and amid shifting demographics in the U.S.
Migration and racialization affect understandings of ethnicity, race, nationality, and their relationships.

Consider the differing experiences of Asian and Black Americans: Asian migrants arrived in the U.S. for many reasons, including fleeing U.S.-imperialism-induced political turmoil and interethnic conflicts, and pursuing better opportunities (Lee, 2015).
text.formatted: Consider the differing experiences of Asian and Black Americans: Asian migrants arrived in the U.S. for many reasons, including fleeing U.S.-imperialism-induced political turmoil and interethnic conflicts, and pursuing better opportunities <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lee, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Given this migration history, Asian Americans often maintain an ethnic identity separate from their racial identity (e.g., Chinese and Asian; Ruiz et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Given this migration history, Asian Americans often maintain an ethnic identity separate from their racial identity (e.g., Chinese and Asian; <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Ruiz et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Some also may only identify ethnically and not racially, even though the pan-Asian label emerged as a political construct in the 1960s to represent and unite various ethnic groups with Asian ancestry under a single superordinate category (Takaki, 1989).
text.formatted: Some also may only identify ethnically and not racially, even though the pan-Asian label emerged as a political construct in the 1960s to represent and unite various ethnic groups with Asian ancestry under a single superordinate category <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Takaki, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, most Black Americans descend from enslaved ancestors, and their ancestral knowledge was systematically erased by the trans-Atlantic slave trade.
However, the "one-drop rule" historically categorized anyone with African ancestry simply as Black (Harris, 1964).
text.formatted: However, the "one-drop rule" historically categorized anyone with African ancestry simply as Black <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Harris, 1964)</ref>.

text.text: In response, a shared history of resistance against oppression has fostered a collective Black diasporic and national identity, making ethnicity and race permeable (Cox & Tamir, 2022).
text.formatted: In response, a shared history of resistance against oppression has fostered a collective Black diasporic and national identity, making ethnicity and race permeable <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cox & Tamir, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, Asian Americans identify strongly with their ethnic groups, whereas Black Americans view race as central to their identity (Budiman & Ruiz, 2021).
text.formatted: Indeed, Asian Americans identify strongly with their ethnic groups, whereas Black Americans view race as central to their identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Budiman & Ruiz, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, different racialization experiences determine how nationality is negotiated in the U.S. and within a broader transnational context involving individuals' ancestral nation-states.

The perpetual foreigner stereotype against Asian Americans, for example, accentuates the boundary between race and nationality, conveniently justifying their exploitation and sociopolitical invisibility (Lee, 2015).
text.formatted: The perpetual foreigner stereotype against Asian Americans, for example, accentuates the boundary between race and nationality, conveniently justifying their exploitation and sociopolitical invisibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lee, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Also, Asian Americans who maintain ties with nations besides the U.S. often navigate their national membership in global, transnational processes (e.g., shaping developments in their ancestral nation-states; Zhou & Gatewood, 2000).
text.formatted: Also, Asian Americans who maintain ties with nations besides the U.S. often navigate their national membership in global, transnational processes (e.g., shaping developments in their ancestral nation-states; <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Zhou & Gatewood, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: While the presence of asylum-and opportunity-seeking Caribbean or African migrants suggests similar ties with non-U.S. nations for Black Americans (Rutland & Batalova, 2025a , 2025b), there is a large population of Black Americans for whom connections to non-U.S. national contexts were involuntarily erased.

text.text: Therefore, there are movements to define Black American nationality as a nation within a nation (e.g., Black nationalism; Robinson, 2001).
text.formatted: Therefore, there are movements to define Black American nationality as a nation within a nation (e.g., Black nationalism; <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Robinson, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Ethnicity, race, and nationality are intricately interrelated, and their manifestation and interaction vary across groups.

The misconception that these identities and their relationship are constant and distinct across social groups prevents engagement with between-group and within-group differences in a nonessentializing, meaningful, and historically grounded way.
Despite recent movements to integrate race and ethnicity, the omission of nationality and the inadequate conceptualization of these identities in ethnicity and race research remain as critical gaps.

To truly center the people at the heart of ethnicity and race research, it is necessary for empirical data to properly document and measure how individuals from different minoritized groups define ethnicity, race, and nationality.
In this study, we examined the lay definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality by 299 Asian American and 284 Black American adults using codebook thematic analysis while integrating reflexivity.
We chose these two groups because of their different migration and racialization patterns.
Additionally, Asian Americans are the fastest-growing racially minoritized group in the U.S. but are invisibilized in psychological research (Vinluan & Remedios, 2024; Budiman & Ruiz, 2021).
text.formatted: Additionally, Asian Americans are the fastest-growing racially minoritized group in the U.S. but are invisibilized in psychological research <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Vinluan & Remedios, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Budiman & Ruiz, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, Black Americans are the second largest racially minoritized population in the U.S., but there is limited research on their, as well as Asian Americans', perceptions of ethnicity, race, and nationality holistically.
We expected there to be both group similarities and differences in identity definitions and their relationships.
Both Asian and Black Americans are considered racial minorities within the U.S., supporting some similarities in how they navigate the connections between ethnicity, race, and nationality.
That said, with the differences in racial experiences and migration patterns, we also expected meaningful variations.

text.text: We restricted our sample to adults residing in the U.S., including U.S. non-citizens, with at least a 95% approval rating on Prolific.com.
Participants received $2.67 USD in compensation for a 20-minute study.
Of the 602 participants that finished our study, 10 participants failed our attention check, i.e., "How many fatal heart attacks have you had?"
The correct answer was zero.
Six participants requested exclusion of their data.
These participants were removed from all analyses, as pre-registered on OSF.
An additional three participants who did not identify as Asian American or Black were removed, for a final sample of 583 participants.
Participants identified as Asian American (n = 299) or Black (n = 284).
Multiracial participants were included in the sample, but were a minority in both the Asian American (n = 5; 1.6%) and Black American samples (n = 9; 3.2%).
No participants identified as both Asian American and Black.

Participants who identified as Asian American further specified their origin group as East Asian (n = 137; 45.8%), Southeast Asian (n = 89; 29.8%), South Asian (n = 56; 18.7%), West Asian (n = 1; 0.3%), other (n = 1; 0.3%), selected multiple groups (n = 14; 4.7%), or did not respond (n = 1; 0.3%).

A majority of participants who identified as Black also identified as African American (n = 195; 68.7%), while a minority identified as Eastern African (n = 4; 1.4%), Central African (n = 1; 0.4%), Southern African (n = 7; 2.5%), Western African (n = 24; 8.5%), Caribbean (n = 8; 2.8%), Afro-Indigenous (n = 5; 1.8%), other (n = 6; 2.1%), selected multiple groups (n = 33; 11.6%), or did not respond (n = 1; 0.4%).

text.text: After passing a botcheck and providing informed consent, participants defined ethnicity, race, and nationality in a random order following this instruction: "People talk about ethnicity, race, and national identity in how they identify.
These identities are intertwined but they are also distinct.
Ethnic, racial, and national identities can all be in line for some people but may not be the case for others.
Briefly, define race, ethnicity, and nationality as you see them.
There are no right or wrong answers."
After providing their definitions, participants responded to additional exploratory items that were not discussed here.
These items included an open-ended question asking participants to detail their "all-encompassing identity," after reading short definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality for added clarity.

Participants also reported whether they self-labeled using ethnic (e.g., Chinese), ethnic American (e.g., Chinese American), pan-ethnic (e.g., Asian), pan-ethnic American (e.g., Asian American), and American labels.
In a random order, participants reported their ethnic identification, U.S. identification, and race centrality.
Participants reported their demographics and read a short debriefing form, where they could indicate whether they wanted to exclude their data without affecting their compensation.
We conducted a codebook thematic analysis, using a structured codebook to extract patterns while accounting for individual variation in participant responses (Braun et al., 2019).

text.text: Taking a subtle realist epistemological stance, we assumed that social experiences exist independently from the subjective mind but could only be detected and interpreted through lenses shaped by researchers' lived experiences (Hammersley, 1992).

text.text: Researchers' positionality to the research topic is essential for helping readers evaluate the analytic process and results.
Two research assistants and the first authors (S.L. and D.J.S.) served as coders.

The first authors were of East Asian descent: S.L. is a 1.5 generation Chinese American cisgender-woman and D.J.S. is a fifth-generation multiracial Japanese American and Irish American cisgender-man.
The two research assistants were of East (Chinese) and Southeast Asian (Filipino American) descent.
Other co-authors (R.M.L. and S.T.J.H.) interpreted and revised the themes during manuscript preparation.
R.M.L. is a second-generation Korean American cisgender-man and S.T.J.H. is a U.S. slave-descendant Black American cisgender-woman.
This team composition was an asset to data analysis.

First, our shared experience with participants as racially minoritized individuals in the U.S., without assuming we fully understood participants' narratives, helped preserve participants' voices during analysis.

Second, our varied lived experience with these identity domains, combined with our academic expertise, ensured that participants' responses were considered through different perspectives and prevented essentialization.
That said, because all coders were Asian-identified, our subjective lens and data interpretation could be different from those of a team of multiracial or Black American coders.
Thus, the results presented in this paper were one of many possible, valid interpretations; they are bound by the coders' lived expertise and blind spots.
Our analysis involved (1) familiarizing ourselves with the data, (2) generating codes, (3) identifying themes, (4) reviewing themes, and (5) defining themes (Braun & Clarke, 2006).

text.text: For each sample, a spreadsheet was created, containing participants' verbatim definitions.
Coders read through all responses at least once.
During data cleaning (e.g., correcting spelling), responses were reviewed again by all coders.
Coders met extensively to clarify the analytic goal: to understand how participants defined ethnicity, race, and nationality.
The following procedures were conducted separately for each sample.
For each identity, coders inductively extracted meaning units (basic ideas) from responses (Merriam, 2009).
text.formatted: For each identity, coders inductively extracted meaning units (basic ideas) from responses <ref type="bibr">(Merriam, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: For example, "Ethnicity is about your culture and lineage" contains two meaning units: "Ethnicity is about culture" and "Ethnicity is about lineage."

Codes were seldom organized to limit latent interpretations before a holistic understanding of the dataset was developed; only identical meaning units were merged for coding efficiency (e.g., "I am Asian" and "Asian").
To ensure consistent attention to details and depth across coders, S.L. discussed the first 50 coded responses for each identity with each responsible coder besides herself (Belotto, 2018).
text.formatted: To ensure consistent attention to details and depth across coders, S.L. discussed the first 50 coded responses for each identity with each responsible coder besides herself <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Belotto, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, coders compiled meaning units into three codebooks, one for each identity.
Once coders finished generating codes and developed a thorough understanding of the responses, they grouped related meaning units into categories, which were then organized into higher-order themes.
The coding team met biweekly to discuss progress codebook development, themes, and diverse views over coding decisions, especially over ambiguous responses.
Next, coders developed coding manuals based on the codebooks.
These manuals retained the category and theme headings, their rationale, and inclusion/exclusion criteria.
For each identity, a coder who was not responsible for building the corresponding codebook conducted hit counts using the manual.
This second coder reviewed the coding manual, read through all responses, and marked the presence or absence of each category using a dichotomized Yes/No ("1"/blank) scale.
Responses were coded for multiple categories under one theme when reflecting multiple connected but distinct ideas.
For instance, a participant received two hits for defining ethnicity in terms of cultural themes if they discussed cultural values and practices.

However, multiple meaning units from the same category within a single response were only coded once, to ensure that frequency represented the prominence of unique ideas rather than repeated phrasing.
After hit counts were completed for all three identity domains, the coders calculated category-and theme-level frequencies for each sample.
Notable themes were highlighted based on generalizability and ability to convey nuances within and between samples (Table 2).

text.text: Themes prominent in only one sample also were discussed.

Across Asian American and Black American samples, we identified shared themes regarding ethnicity including cultural components; heritage, ancestry, or family; defining ethnicity in relation to race; and country or geographic location.
Social traits (Asian American) and shared identity or belonging (Black American) were only prominent in one sample.
Cultural Components.

Across samples, cultural elements including language, customs, traditions, religion, values, clothing, food, and other culturally specific characteristics were key for understanding ethnicity ("a person's common cultural-linguistic traits").

Participants viewed ethnicity as rooted in cultural practices ("...cultural practices and beliefs people have and celebrate") and symbolic expressions that distinguish groups ("...cultural identification of different people in the different parts of the world.").
Heritage, Ancestry, or Family.
Mentions of heritage, ancestry, or family were common, highlighting generational ties.
Participants described ethnicity as passed down in families and embedded in lineage ("your heritage like parental background").
Emphases on ancestral or familial connections to culture, nation, or region suggested a relational view of ethnicity.
Both samples referenced race when defining ethnicity.

Some saw ethnicity and race as interchangeable ("ethnicity is similar to race"), while others viewed them as distinct ("someone's race could be Asian, but their ethnicity is Indian") or linked ("similar to race but more focused on cultural belonging").
Multiple Asian American participants characterized ethnicity as a "subcategory" or the "breakdown" of race, conceptualizing ethnicity as more specific or narrow than race.

In comparison, while Black American participants described ethnicity as "stemming from" or "based on" race, they were more ambiguous about the property of their relationship (e.g., one being narrower than the other).
These patterns reflected shared efforts to define ethnicity through the lens of racial categorization, but the more nuanced understanding of their associations varied.
Both samples defined ethnicity by referencing a specific country or region.

Some codes mentioned both culture and geography; these were included under this theme when participants clearly conceptualized culture as existing within the confines of a country or geographic area (e.g., "ethnicity is defined by the culture of my country of origin.").
This theme highlighted how ethnic identity could be anchored in a physical place.
Social traits or processes (Asian American).
Unique to the Asian American sample, the theme social traits or processes captured definitions of ethnicity that emphasized its social nature and function.

Participants explicitly used the term "social" when describing ethnicity as a social identity, as a group-based belonging ("…the way we describe the social group…that one belongs to."), or as an identity maintained through interactions or shared experiences ("Ethnicity differentiates on the [basis] of…social events."
; "A term that refers to…experiences shared by a group of people.").
This theme underscored the understanding of ethnicity as dynamic and shaped through social processes.
Among Black American participants, this theme represented a sense of collective identity, belonging, and connectedness-being part of something larger than oneself.

It included notions of community, systems of inclusion, and the emotional experience of being part of a shared group ("…a source of pride, solidarity, diversity, and belonging for many people."; "…a quality or fact of belonging to a population group or subgroup.").
These responses emphasized the social and affective dimensions of ethnicity as a source of solidarity and mutual recognition within this sample.
Across samples, overlapping themes regarding race included physical, genetic, or biological traits; ancestral traits; region of origin; and social construct.
The Asian American sample uniquely emphasized cultural traits, while the Black American sample highlighted the grouping of people and ethnicity.
Shared physical, genetic, or biological traits.
Participants commonly defined race in terms of physical or biological characteristics, including skin color, facial features, hair texture, and body shape.
Responses explicitly referencing physical traits, biological features, or genetic makeup were included in this category.
For some participants, race was linked to genetic composition or DNA ("...
I am black because the majority of my genetic makeup is identical to the DNA of people from a few different regions in Africa"), indicating a biological understanding of racial categorization.
Participants described race in terms of origin, history, and family background ("…an idea that splits humans into certain groups of origin based on ancestral origin").

Responses often referenced hereditary traits or lineages ("…how one categorizes themselves based on their parents"), and some referred to genetic inheritance passed through family lines ("...categorizing people into distinct groups based on physical characteristics such as skin color, facial features, and hair texture…linked to ancestry, heritage, and shared genetic traits amongst a particular set of people.").
This theme was unified by the conceptualization of race as transmitted through ancestry and familial continuity.
Participants in both samples defined race through regional origins.
Race was understood as reflecting "where one comes from" or the area associated with a particular group's heritage or genetic background.

Some participants left the notion of "origin" unspecified, while others tied it to geography or the region from which one's lineage or genetic composition derived ("the different adaptations we've gained based on regional differences").
This theme highlighted the spatial and locational framing of race as a marker of group difference.
Social construct.
This theme captured the understanding of race as a human-made, socially-defined concept.

Participants described race as created by society, man-made, or socially constructed, reflecting awareness of sociopolitical processes ("...reinforced by social norms and institutions") that shape racial categories and their meanings.
For example, one Black participant wrote, "[Race is] a social construct.
We are all different colors, even what they call Black people, but I don't think it's a race."
Another Asian participant wrote, "...race is primarily a social construct and lacks a universally agreed-upon definition.
Different societies and cultures have developed their own ways of categorizing and understanding race."

Interestingly, in both samples, this theme often co-occurred with themes like shared physical, biological, or genetic traits (e.g., "…a social construct based on skin color") and a grouping of people (e.g., "…a social construction to help better identify ourselves.
For example, I am Black; someone I know is White.").

On the other hand, whereas it often co-occurred with themes about discrimination in the Black American sample (e.g., "…a flawed and arbitrary concept that has been used to perpetuate inequality, discrimination, and social hierarchies"), there were no mentions of stereotype, prejudice, racism, or discrimination in responses coded for the social construct theme in the Asian American sample.
Cultural Traits (Asian American).
This theme reflected a conceptualization of race grounded in shared culture, independent from (although often concurrent with) biological or geographic features.
Participants in this category defined race by common cultural backgrounds ("…the umbrella term for your cultural background." and "…the categorization of people based on common cultural traits.").
Notably, mentions of culture in Asian American participants' race definitions were typically nondescript ("cultural identities", "cultural separation", "cultural ancestry").
This vagueness was noticeably different from the multidimensional descriptions seen in the ethnicity definitions.

Combined with the fact that these respondents did not link culture to a particular country or nationality, the results suggested an understanding of race as overlapping with, but not reducible to, ethnic or cultural identity.
This theme mainly included two types of responses.
First was the function or purpose of the concept of race: namely, to categorize, classify, or divide people into distinct groups.
The second type was more descriptive, identifying specific racial groups (e.g., "Asian," "Black") or explicitly defining race as "groups of people" or "racial gatherings."
Together, these responses framed race as a structural and social mechanism for grouping or differentiating individuals.
This theme reflected an understanding of race as closely related to ("race goes hand in hand with ethnicity") or interchangeable with ethnicity ("race is whichever ethnicity you were born into").
Similar to earlier definitions of ethnicity, there was no consensus on how race and ethnicity were linked.
One participant wrote, "Race is a more broad term than ethnicity.", whereas another wrote, "Race is similar to me as ethnicity is."
The discourse extended to perceived mechanisms that connected or differentiated these two identity domains.

Some believed that race was defined by genetically-or phenotypically-determined ethnic membership ("race is what ethnic group you are genetically a part of"); others believed the focus on shared biological characteristics-often along with a weaker focus on culture-was exactly what differentiated race from ethnicity ("race is a bit like ethnicity but I feel like it's slightly different because you can be black but not align with the certain cultures that represent the black community so I think race is more of a color thing").

One participant believed race is phenotypically-based but becomes closely connected to ethnicity because race-based perceptions has social and cultural impact: "Race is phenotype only THOUGH I think it can be considered an ethnicity too since [people] judge you based off your race and you may have certain cultural norms due to this that differ from others."
One interpretation of this statement was that they perceived race-based experiences to shape ethnic identities.

The codes under this theme indicated that some participants understood race by using ethnicity as a simile (i.e., equate the two), an analogy (i.e., highlight properties of ethnicity that also hold for race), or a reference point for derivation (i.e., use ethnicity as a starting point for conceptualizing race and then differentiate).
Across samples, overlapping themes included region of birth/origin; country of belonging or affiliation; legal and political factors; place of residence; and pledge, duty, and rights.

One caveat was that, in this section, a few participants (n < 10) generated elaborate responses similar in structure (e.g., mentioning birth, descent, and naturalization in the same order); most came from the Black American sample.
