text.text: Although our data collection (early 2023) predated the popularization of AI-powered search tools (e.g., Gemini, OpenAI), it was possible that some participants researched the definition of nationality when answering this question.
These responses were included for three reasons.
First, both samples were well-educated and > 55% of the respondents had attained a college degree or higher, increasing the likelihood of sophisticated civic knowledge.
text.formatted: First, both samples were well-educated and > 55% of the respondents had attained a college degree or higher, increasing the likelihood of sophisticated civic knowledge.

text.text: Second, there were no identical responses, and removing responses based on similarity would be antithetical to using a codebook and conducting hit counts.
Third, as long as the participants autonomously supplied the definition, they followed the instructions.
Region of Birth/Origin.
Region of birth or origin was a central way of defining nationality.
Participants commonly described nationality as a birthright: something determined by where one was born or spent their early life ("If you were born in America, your nationality is U.S. American.").

This definition emphasized nationality as fixed and established at the beginning of life, representing one's geographic and social origin ("Nationality can be [a] composite of regional location and national origins…where the person was born.").
Both samples associated nationality with the sense of belonging, affiliation, or emotional connection to a country.
Importantly, these meanings extended beyond legal or political status.

For instance, statements such as "[Nationality is] where your heart belongs" and "Nationality is the country that you feel a sense of connection with" illustrated an internal, affective dimension of national identity.
Participants distinguished between formal membership (e.g., citizenship) and an experiential sense of belonging, highlighting the subjective and identity-based aspect of nationality.
Legal and Political Factors.
This theme captured definitions of nationality based on formal legal relationships with a country.

Some participants mentioned abstract, general political ties and rights (e.g., "…the legal and political relationship between an individual and a particular nation-state."; "…the legal…cultural identity of a person that belongs to a specific country.").
Other participants referred to specific legal and political affiliations that signify national membership, such as having citizenship or holding a passport.
Notably, Asian American participants referenced citizenship much more frequently than Black American participants.
Some responses containing this theme explicitly clarified that the conceptualization of nationality as grounded in legal or political factors may or may not have to do with ethnicity and race.
One participant wrote, "Nationality would be of whatever country that one is a legal and permanent citizen of.
This applies to a Black, Mexican, or Indian person regardless of ancestry."
In contrast, another participant wrote that, "Nationality is ethnicity."
Besides sharing their own definitions, some participants believed nationality's perceived relation to other social identities differs across individuals and contexts.
One wrote, "Depending on the laws of the nation, nationality may require ethnic inclusion or could be disconnected [from] any other form of social identity."
Another person wrote, "[Nationality is] also wildly misunderstood as being ethnicity by a lot of people."

This theme underscored the institutional dimension of nationality as defined through laws and governance structures, which sometimes occurred with different opinions on its tie to other identity domains, such as ethnicity.
This theme described where one currently lives or has lived ("...where one is residing").
Some participants emphasized the importance of having been raised or having lived for an extended duration in a country for residence to constitute nationality.
This theme reflected an experiential understanding of nationality tied to residency-based familiarity.
Pledge, Duty, and Rights.

In both samples, some participants defined nationality in terms of one's duties (e.g., abiding by national laws), responsibilities (e.g., civic participation), and rights (e.g., voting, access to social services).
Some participants considered these elements interdependent, viewing rights and duties as mutually reinforcing.
For instance, voting was mentioned as both a right of citizenship and a responsibility of national membership.
This theme highlighted the civic and moral dimensions of nationality, positioning it as a privilege and an obligation.
Notably, this theme was coded much more frequently in the Black American sample than in the Asian American sample.
Examination of individual responses with relevant codes in both samples were similar in the degree of specificity and substantiveness.

Psychological research and practice have largely treated ethnicity, race, and nationality as separable constructs, a default that constrains both the discipline's explanatory power and the validity of instruments built on it.
To explore how this default approach may be revised, we thematically analyzed lay definitions of ethnicity, race, and nationality from 299 Asian American and 284 Black American adults.
First, we found similarities and meaningful differences in these groups' identity definitions and perceived relationships among identities.
The variations in ethnicity and race definitions may be understood by considering migration and racialization patterns and racial formation as a dynamic process (Omi & Winant, 2014).

text.text: Many Asian American participants described ethnicity as nested within race because ethnicity may become how individuals differentiate within the "Asian" umbrella category, particularly in contexts where interethnic distinctions are salient (Espiritu, 1992).

text.text: Conversely, many Black American participants conflated ethnicity and race as synonymous, which may be due to ancestral erasure through slavery and hypodescent (i.e., assigning individuals of multiracial ancestry to the racial group with lower social status), as well as experiencing "Blackness" as a culture rooted in resistance, strengths, and perseverance against racism (Johnson & Carter, 2020; Winston & Kittles, 2005).

text.text: Differential racialization experiences also help clarify how Asian and Black Americans distinctively defined nationality.
For both, nationality included belonging, affiliation, residence, and political-legal elements.

But Asian Americans' emphasis on citizenship or legal status and Black Americans' emphasis on civic duty and rights may originate from these groups being deemed foreign and being denied full civic and social participation, respectively (Zou & Cheryan, 2017).

text.text: Critically, anchoring nationality in legal legitimacy and in civic relations are not mutually exclusive.
Both demonstrate that national belonging has to be negotiated and could be weaponized to maintain the racial status quo (Ngai, 2004).
text.formatted: Both demonstrate that national belonging has to be negotiated and could be weaponized to maintain the racial status quo <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Ngai, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Also, because most Asian American participants identified as first-(foreign-born) and second-generation (domestic-born but with at least one foreign-born parent), they likely had personal or vicarious experiences of being barred or discouraged from civic participation (e.g., inability to vote or use social services; Tran, 2018).

text.text: Second, we found that ethnicity, race, and nationality are interconnected, with blurred boundaries and content: geographic locations defined all three identities, and ethnicity and race were mutual reference points for defining each other.
This finding aligned with research documenting the conflation of ethnicity and race, and the racial implications of nationality (Cornell & Hartmann, 2007; Devos & Banaji, 2005).

text.text: Because the boundaries among these identities are socially constructed, theorizing them as having fixed or inherent boundaries could lead to fragmented knowledge across disciplinary and regional lines (Brubaker, 2009).

text.text: Together, these results called for conceptualizing ethnicity, race, and nationality in tandem.

Additionally, Sellers et al. (1998) emphasized that racial identity takes meaning within group-specific contexts, and Yamamoto (1995) described how all racial groups provide dynamic identity reference points for one another.

(1998)</ref> emphasized that racial identity takes meaning within group-specific contexts, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Yamamoto (1995)</ref> described how all racial groups provide dynamic identity reference points for one another.

text.text: Our findings supported and extended these calls.

Although many responses described prejudice and discrimination, they rarely addressed Whiteness explicitly, suggesting that comparison with a majority group is one of several ways minoritized individuals make sense of their identities.

Definitions in our samples were best understood through group-specific contexts, dynamic interactions with multi-group environments, and shared identity-formation processes (Kim, 1999; Phinney, 1992).

text.text: This pattern underscored the need to balance these contexts and processes while integrating ethnicity, race, and nationality as a unit of analysis, work that remains much needed (Brubaker, 2009).

text.text: Our results have several theoretical implications: first, conceptualizing race, ethnicity, and nationality in tandem can strengthen the literature's explanatory power on U.S.-based civic engagement that varies across ethnic and racial lines.

Given the varied definitions of these social identities, considering the shifting ethnic and racial composition of the U.S. population, research should explore the applicability of identity constructs across groups.
For example, whereas race centrality is theorized as a crucial component of Black identity (Sellers, 1998), ethnicity centrality may be a more meaningful construct for Asian Americans.
text.formatted: For example, whereas race centrality is theorized as a crucial component of Black identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Sellers, 1998)</ref>, ethnicity centrality may be a more meaningful construct for Asian Americans.

text.text: Also, an intra-minority perspective could be beneficial for the U.S. context by accounting for intra-minority processes that help maintain the status quo; an example is how Asian Americans are valorized to justify anti-Black racism, while being rendered foreign and civically ostracized compared to White people (Kim, 1999).
text.formatted: Also, an intra-minority perspective could be beneficial for the U.S. context by accounting for intra-minority processes that help maintain the status quo; an example is how Asian Americans are valorized to justify anti-Black racism, while being rendered foreign and civically ostracized compared to White people <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kim, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Contemporary moments of heightened racial tension, including the intensified anti-Asian rhetoric during the COVID-19 pandemic or public discourse around affirmative action, illustrate how narratives about intra-minority relations can be activated to fracture solidarity or to maintain hierarchies (Jagpal & Schumacher, 2022).

text.text: Critically, if intra-minority interaction is part of how racial meanings are reproduced, then it can also be a mechanism to build intergroup solidarity (Yamamoto, 1995).

text.text: Although we did not measure intergroup attitudes, coalition behavior, or political participation, these perspectives are raised as implications and directions for future work rather than causal claims.
Second, nation or nationality provides an ecological context in ethnicity-and race-based processes that should be explicitly and extensively examined.

Meaningful engagement with participants' identity definitions was made by considering U.S.-specific conditions of migration and racialization, suggesting that the national context shapes identity meaning-making.
Recent scholarship has expanded to study ethnicity and race in non-U.S. and transnational contexts (e.g., experiences of racialization after migration; Juang et al. 2020).
text.formatted: Recent scholarship has expanded to study ethnicity and race in non-U.S. and transnational contexts (e.g., experiences of racialization after migration; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Juang et al. 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This trend warrants the explicit inclusion of nationality in ethnicity and race research because every national context is unique in its migration patterns, legislation, media representation, and popular cultural narratives pertaining to social group and hierarchy formation.

Cross-national research is most likely to produce valid and relevant knowledge after examining the construct validity of ethnicity, race, and nationality in each new national context where U.S.-based ethnicity and race theories are adopted.
A context-sensitive, linked-domains approach helps evaluate when and how U.S.-derived theories travel, require adaptation, or fail to capture local dynamics.
The results also have practical implications.
First, they help explain the inconsistent connection between ethnic/racial identity development and well-being across races.

Ethnic identity dimensions correlate with well-being and health outcomes, but the effect sizes vary across racial groups (Rivas-Drake et al., 2014; Yip et al., 2019), and ethnic-racial identity's protective effect on mental health after discrimination also varies (Woo et al., 2019; Yip et al., 2019).

text.text: Construct nonequivalence may explain these variations: these identity domains are not stable with distinguishable boundaries or defined identically across groups (Harachi et al., 2006; Kline, 2005).
text.formatted: Construct nonequivalence may explain these variations: these identity domains are not stable with distinguishable boundaries or defined identically across groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Harachi et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Kline, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Scales developed assuming construct equivalence may capture different processes, producing heterogeneous relations with health outcomes.
Conceptualizing and measuring these identities as linked may reconcile mixed findings and increase data interpretability.
Second, nationality and racialization appear intertwined.

Considering nationality in measures of organizational inclusion, political and institutional messaging, coalition behaviors, and interracial attitudes may clarify how perceived linkage among identity domains influences real-world participation professionally, socially, and civically.

Implementation of this idea into practice could look like disaggregating ethnic, racial, and national data-preserving the distinct insights each provides for organizing and advocacy-while avoiding the assumptions that these identities function independently in measurement, clinical, educational, and workplace settings.

Simultaneously, raising public awareness of the socially constructed nature of these identities and developing coalition-building interventions and civic outreach that address intra-minority dynamics within a White-dominant society (e.g., comparative stereotypes, scarcity mindsets), may open door for solidarity and collective action toward equity for all.

The Black American sample may not adequately reflect the experience of immigrants and refugees due to limited representation, constraining inferences about how ethnicity, race, and nationality are conceptualized across diverse Black American communities.

Similarly, the Asian American sample was overrepresentative of East Asian participants relative to both Southeast Asian and South Asian participants and no ethnic information aside from regional categorization was collected (e.g., Filipino versus Southeast Asian; Vinluan & Remedios, 2024).
text.formatted: Similarly, the Asian American sample was overrepresentative of East Asian participants relative to both Southeast Asian and South Asian participants and no ethnic information aside from regional categorization was collected (e.g., Filipino versus Southeast Asian; <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Vinluan & Remedios, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The overrepresentation of East Asian participants and how participants were categorized may have influenced the themes that emerged, even though it was not our goal to detect within-sample differences.

Future research should utilize larger, more diverse samples with more detailed demographic assessments and use additional methodologies (e.g., cognitive interviewing, quantitative methods) to investigate the relationship between lay definitions of different identities, perceptions of their relationships, and downstream outcomes (e.g., civic engagement, mental health, belonging), and capture heterogeneity within each racial group.
Finally, several participants provided elaborate, similar nationality definitions, raising the possibility that they consulted external sources.
If so, these participants' personal views could not be discerned from academic sources.

However, seeking information is a normal and necessary learning activity to develop understandings of social identities and eliminating these responses may eliminate participants who attempted this question in good faith but felt they lacked relevant insights.

Overall, the present study indicates that ethnicity, race, and nationality are intertwined identities whose meanings and boundaries vary across and within racially minoritized groups in patterns that may be historically and socially situated.

Attending to these linked meanings has important implications for developing more ecologically valid ethnicity and race frameworks, improving measurement validity, defying the assumed universality or total idiosyncrasy of identity processes, and informing better practices (e.g., programming, education, and healthcare).
